title: Motivational interviewing — drinking (session 2)

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Last time you mentioned you weren't sure whether you wanted to talk about the drinking. Where are you with that today?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Honestly, my partner thinks it's a problem. I'm not convinced. Everyone has a few drinks after work.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: It feels like your partner is more worried than you are.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, I don't drink in the mornings or anything. I go to work.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: You're holding things together, and that matters to you. And at the same time something brought you back here today.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Well, the thing is, last Saturday I don't really remember getting home. That scared me a bit.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Not remembering getting home scared you.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yeah. And my daughter saw me like that. She's nine.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: What was that like, knowing she saw you?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Awful. She asked me on Sunday if I was sick. I said yes.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Part of you says it's normal, everyone drinks. Another part of you felt awful when your daughter asked if you were sick.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: That's it exactly. I don't want her to see me like that.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Being the kind of parent you want to be is really important to you.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: It's the most important thing.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: If you decided to make a change, what might that look like? Not what you should do — what you might want.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Maybe not drinking at weekends when I have her. That would be a start.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: You'd like to not drink on the weekends you have your daughter.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I think I could do that. Weeknights are different, that's my time to relax.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: So weekends with your daughter feel possible, and weeknights still feel like your way of unwinding. That's your call to make.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yeah. Maybe later I'd think about weeknights. Not yet.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: On a scale of zero to ten, how important is it to you to make the weekend change?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Nine.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: And how confident are you that you could do it?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Maybe six.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Six, not three. What makes it a six?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I've done it before, when I was training for a run. I didn't drink for two months.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: You've already shown you can do it for two months when you had a reason that mattered.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I forgot about that, actually.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: What would help take it from six to seven?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Maybe telling my partner the plan. And not having wine in the house on Fridays.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: So the plan you've come to is no drinking on weekends with your daughter, telling your partner, and keeping wine out of the house on Fridays. How does that sound to you?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: It sounds like something I could actually do.

expected_note_facts: Client reports partner is concerned about drinking; client ambivalent
Client could not remember getting home last Saturday; found this frightening
Client's nine-year-old daughter saw client intoxicated and asked if client was sick
Previously abstained for two months while training for a run
Plan: no alcohol on weekends with daughter; tell partner; no wine in house on Fridays

strengths: Double-sided reflection of ambivalence (normal vs felt awful)
Affirmed client's value of being a good parent
Used importance/confidence scaling and asked 'why six not three'
missed_openings: The memory blackout could have been explored a little more with permission
Weeknight drinking 'to relax' could later be explored for what it does for the client
try_next: Ask permission before offering information, e.g. about blackouts

review: CLINICAL-REVIEW: synthetic role-play; drafts for the Clinical Lead.
